title: Design a Number Container System
description: Brute force to optimized: a full rescan on every find versus a min-heap per number using the lazy deletion pattern.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Design a number container system supporting: change(index, number), which fills the container at index with number (replacing whatever was there before, if anything); and find(number), which returns the SMALLEST index currently holding number, or -1 if number does not currently appear anywhere in the system.

blocks.caption: A min-heap of indices per number, combined with a source-of-truth index-to-number map, answers find() by lazily discarding stale (overwritten) entries

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A sequence of change(index, number) and find(number) calls"],["Output","For each find call, the smallest index currently holding that number, or -1"],["Goal","Support both operations efficiently, even as indices get repeatedly overwritten with different numbers"],["Constraints","1 <= index, number <= 10^9; at most 10^5 calls total to change and find"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Need the SMALLEST index for a given number, repeatedly, as the system changes","A min-heap (priority queue) per number naturally provides fast access to the smallest candidate index"],["An index can be OVERWRITTEN with a different number, invalidating its old entry","A \"lazy deletion\" pattern: never eagerly remove a stale entry from a heap; instead, detect and discard it only when it would otherwise be returned"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Every index holds AT MOST one number at a time, but that number can change repeatedly via change(); find() needs the smallest index CURRENTLY holding a given number, meaning any index that WAS given that number but has since been overwritten must be correctly excluded.

blocks.title: Analogy: Lockers Whose Contents Change, With a Directory of "Which Lockers Have Item X"
blocks.text: Imagine numbered lockers, each holding at most one labeled item at a time, with a directory tracking "which lockers currently contain item X" for quick lookup. When an item is placed in a locker (possibly replacing whatever was there), the directory for the OLD item is not immediately updated (too slow to search and remove); instead, the directory simply keeps a record that might occasionally be OUT OF DATE, and stale entries are simply skipped over and discarded the next time someone actually looks them up.

blocks.caption: change() pushes onto a heap without ever cleaning up stale entries; find() lazily pops (and discards) any stale entries encountered until a genuinely current one surfaces

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: change(2,10), change(1,10), find(10), change(1,20), find(10)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","State","Result"],"rows":[["change(2,10)","index 2 holds 10","-"],["change(1,10)","index 1 holds 10; indices 1 and 2 both hold 10","-"],["find(10)","Smallest index holding 10","1"],["change(1,20)","index 1 now holds 20 (overwritten); only index 2 still holds 10","-"],["find(10)","Index 1's OLD \"holds 10\" record is now stale; only index 2 genuinely holds 10","2"]]}

blocks.text: 5. How Should We Think?

Before eagerly searching for and removing an index's OLD number-association on every change() call (expensive, since a heap does not support fast arbitrary removal), notice that stale entries can simply be left in place and discarded LAZILY, only when they would actually interfere with a find() result.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A separate min-heap PER NUMBER, holding indices, directly supports "give me the smallest index" in O(log n), exactly what find() needs.

Observation 2: When change(index, number) is called, simply pushing the index onto number's heap is easy; but if that index PREVIOUSLY held a DIFFERENT number, that old heap still contains a now-stale entry for index, which is expensive to remove immediately (heaps do not support efficient arbitrary removal).

Observation 3: Instead of removing it immediately, a SEPARATE source-of-truth map (index -> current number) can always confirm whether a given heap entry is still ACTUALLY valid.

Observation 4: When find(number) is called, repeatedly check the heap's current top: if the source-of-truth map disagrees (that index no longer actually holds this number), simply POP it away (lazy deletion) and check again, until a genuinely valid top is found (or the heap empties).
This is the "lazy deletion" pattern applied to a min-heap: stale entries are never proactively removed, only discarded lazily when a query would otherwise return them.
6. Brute Force Solution
Maintain only a plain map from index to its current number; for find(number), scan the ENTIRE map every time, collecting all indices holding that number and taking the minimum.
Step by step algorithm

items: change(index, number) simply updates the map directly.
find(number) scans every entry in the map, filtering for ones matching number, and returns the minimum index among them (or -1 if none).

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A plain map directly and simply tracks each index's current number, with change() being trivially O(1).
find() rescans everything, which is correct but ignores that most indices are IRRELEVANT to a specific query (they hold different numbers entirely).

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Correctly finds the smallest matching index, since a full scan always sees every currently-valid entry.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for change; O(n) for find, scanning every stored index.
Space: O(n), for the map.

Limitation: find()'s O(n) full rescan is wasteful, especially if only a small fraction of indices hold the queried number; a min-heap per number, with lazy deletion, achieves logarithmic find() time instead.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rescans everything on every find() call. Instead, maintain a min-heap PER NUMBER, holding candidate indices. change(index, number) updates the source-of-truth map AND pushes index onto number's heap (without touching the OLD number's heap at all, leaving a stale entry there). find(number) repeatedly checks number's heap top against the source-of-truth map, lazily popping away any stale (no-longer-valid) entries until a genuinely current one is found.

Maintain indexToNum (a plain map) and numToHeap (a map from number to a min-heap of indices). change(index, number): update indexToNum[index] = number; push index onto numToHeap[number]. find(number): if numToHeap has no entry for number, return -1; otherwise, while the heap's top index no longer maps to number in indexToNum, pop it; return the heap's top (or -1 if now empty).
9. Optimized Solution
Use a min-heap per number, combined with a source-of-truth map, lazily discarding stale heap entries only when a find() query would otherwise return them.
Dry run for change(2,10), change(1,10), find(10), change(1,20), find(10)

New top=2: indexToNum[2]=10, matches: valid","-","2"]]}

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The two find(10) calls correctly return 1 and 2, matching the expected results.

codes.python:
import heapq
from collections import defaultdict

class NumberContainers:
    def __init__(self):
        self.index_to_num = {}                                              # the SOURCE OF TRUTH: what number is CURRENTLY at each index
        self.num_to_heap = defaultdict(list)                                # a min-heap of indices per number (may contain STALE entries)

    def change(self, index, number):
        self.index_to_num[index] = number
        heapq.heappush(self.num_to_heap[number], index)                    # just push; never bother removing the OLD number's stale entry

    def find(self, number):
        heap = self.num_to_heap.get(number)
        if not heap:
            return -1
        while heap and self.index_to_num.get(heap[0]) != number:           # lazily discard indices that no longer actually hold this number
            heapq.heappop(heap)
        return heap[0] if heap else -1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nc = NumberContainers()
    nc.change(2, 10)
    nc.change(1, 10)
    print(nc.find(10))
    nc.change(1, 20)
    print(nc.find(10))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n) for change (a single heap push); O(log n) AMORTIZED for find (each stale entry is popped at most once, ever, across its entire lifetime).
Space: O(n), across all the per-number heaps (which may temporarily hold stale entries).
Why This Works

The source-of-truth map (indexToNum) always reflects the CURRENT, correct state, so checking a heap entry against it instantly reveals whether that entry is still valid. Since each change() call can make AT MOST one prior heap entry stale (the index's previous number's heap entry), and each stale entry is only ever popped ONCE (never re-examined after being discarded), the total amount of "wasted" lazy-deletion work across the entire run is bounded by the total number of change() calls, keeping the amortized cost low.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["change(index, number) when index is new or unused","Simply recorded and pushed; no stale entries created"],["change(index, number) when index previously held a DIFFERENT number","That old number's heap now has one stale entry for index, left in place until lazily discovered"],["find(number) encounters a stale top","Popped and discarded; the check repeats against the new top"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: The heap is NEVER proactively cleaned when an index is overwritten; only find() ever discovers and removes stale entries, which is the essence of the lazy deletion pattern.
Checking heap.get(number) or an equivalent existence check before accessing the heap avoids errors when a number has never been associated with any index.
Each stale entry, once popped, is gone forever; it is never re-pushed or re-encountered, which is why the amortized analysis holds.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (plain map, full rescan on find)","O(1) change, O(n) find","O(n)","Simple, but find() ignores that only a fraction of indices are relevant to any given query"],["Optimized (min-heap per number, lazy deletion)","O(log n) change, O(log n) amortized find","O(n)","Uses lazy deletion to avoid expensive eager removal from a heap"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

When a heap-based structure needs to support values becoming "stale" (invalidated by later updates), and heaps do not support efficient arbitrary removal, the LAZY DELETION pattern (check validity against a source-of-truth on access, discarding stale entries only when actually encountered) avoids expensive eager cleanup while remaining correct.
Common mistakes

items: Attempting to eagerly remove a stale entry from a heap on every change() call, which is expensive (heaps do not support efficient arbitrary-element removal).
Forgetting to maintain the source-of-truth map (indexToNum), which is what makes it possible to DETECT a stale heap entry in the first place.
Using a single global heap (not one per number), which would make find(number) unable to efficiently isolate just that number's candidates.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["find() called for a number that was never associated with any index","Correctly returns -1, since no heap exists for it at all"],["An index repeatedly overwritten with the SAME number multiple times","Multiple heap entries for the same index accumulate, but they are all equally \"valid\" (all point to the current number), so no incorrect behavior results, just some redundant entries"],["Every index eventually overwritten to a different number, leaving the original number's heap fully stale","find() correctly pops through and discards ALL of them, eventually returning -1"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly naming the technique ("lazy deletion") and explaining WHY it is needed (heaps lack efficient arbitrary removal) demonstrates recognizing this as a specific, well-known pattern, not an ad-hoc workaround.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Need the MINIMUM (or maximum) of a dynamically changing set, where entries can be invalidated by other operations" points toward a min-heap with LAZY DELETION, checked against a source-of-truth map.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: Why not use a sorted set (like a balanced BST) instead of a heap, which would support proper removal? A sorted set could work and would avoid stale entries entirely, though many languages' standard libraries make a heap-plus-lazy-deletion pattern simpler to implement correctly and efficiently.

What is the worst-case total space usage, given that stale entries accumulate? Bounded by the total number of change() calls across the entire run, since each call adds at most one new heap entry (and invalidates at most one old one).

How would you extend this to also support DELETING an index entirely (not just changing its number)? Simply removing it from indexToNum (or marking it as "no number") would make its existing heap entries permanently stale, correctly handled by the exact same lazy-deletion check on future find() calls.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: The lazy deletion pattern, a technique that generalizes to any priority-queue-based structure needing to handle externally-invalidated entries, distinct from the eager-removal techniques seen in most other stack/queue problems in this project.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(1) change, O(n) find; O(n) space.
Optimized (min-heap per number, lazy deletion): O(log n) change, O(log n) amortized find; O(n) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Min-heap per key, with lazy deletion via a source-of-truth map
Core Idea: change() pushes onto a heap without cleaning up old entries; find() lazily pops away any heap-top entries that no longer match the source-of-truth map, until a genuinely valid one surfaces
Time: O(log n) change, O(log n) amortized find
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Each stale entry is only ever discovered and discarded ONCE, ever, which is what keeps the amortized cost low despite never eagerly cleaning up
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: change: push to numToHeap[number], update indexToNum. find: pop stale heap tops (mismatched in indexToNum) until valid
